name: DHS Case Management Pilot Program (CMPP) — Services for Noncitizens
description: The DHS Case Management Pilot Program (CMPP) provides voluntary case management and other critical services to eligible noncitizens in the United States. Managed by a National Board chaired by DHS and composed of experienced nonprofits (Church World Service, Catholic Charities USA, and The Center for Migration Studies of New York), the program funds local organizations and governments to deliver trauma-informed services including mental health care, trafficking screening, legal orientation programs, cultural orientation, connections to social services, and departure planning. The program specifically serves non-detained noncitizens known to ICE, including individuals who have been paroled, released on bond, enrolled in Alternatives to Detention programs, or issued a Notice to Appear. Services are voluntary and designed to help participants navigate the immigration process while meeting basic needs.
eligibility: Non-detained noncitizens known to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including individuals who have been paroled, released on bond, in Alternatives to Detention programs, or issued a Notice to Appear; participation is voluntary
amount: No direct funding to individuals; program provides free case management and social services through funded local organizations
applicationProcess: Contact a CMPP-funded service provider in your area. Participation is voluntary and services are offered free of charge. Referrals may come through ICE, local nonprofits, or community organizations. Participants receive individualized case management plans that may include mental health support, legal orientation, cultural adjustment, and connections to local social services.
geographicScope: United States — services delivered through local nonprofits and community organizations funded by the CMPP National Board in select locations nationwide
documentsRequired: Government-issued identification or immigration documents; proof of immigration status or pending proceedings; specific requirements may vary by local service provider

name: ORR Matching Grant Program — Refugee Early Employment
description: The ORR Matching Grant Program is a public-private partnership that helps refugees and other ORR-eligible populations achieve economic self-sufficiency through early employment within 240 days of arrival, without accessing public cash assistance programs such as TANF or SSI. For every $1 raised by participating resettlement agencies through cash donations, in-kind services, or volunteer support, ORR awards $2 in federal funding (up to $2,020 per client). The program provides intensive employment services including job readiness training, resume preparation, interview coaching, job placement assistance, and post-employment follow-up. Participants also receive case management, English language training referrals, and support navigating cultural adjustment in the workplace. The program is operated through national voluntary resettlement agencies including Church World Service, HIAS, International Rescue Committee, Lutheran Immigration and Refugee Service, and others.
eligibility: Refugees, asylees, Cuban/Haitian entrants, Special Immigrant Visa holders, certified victims of trafficking, and other ORR-eligible populations; must enroll within 31 days of arrival or eligibility date; must not be receiving TANF, SSI, or other public cash assistance
amount: Up to $2,020 per participant in federal matching funds ($2 federal for every $1 raised by agency); plus employment services, training, and case management at no cost
applicationProcess: Contact a participating national voluntary resettlement agency (VOLAG) such as Church World Service, HIAS, IRC, or LIRS within 31 days of your arrival or eligibility date. Complete an intake assessment and enroll in the Matching Grant program. You will be assigned a case manager who will work with you on job readiness, resume building, interview skills, and job placement. Employment must be achieved within 240 days. Post-employment support is provided for job retention.
geographicScope: United States — nationwide through participating voluntary resettlement agencies and their local affiliates
documentsRequired: Proof of ORR-eligible immigration status (I-94, refugee travel document, asylee documentation, SIV documentation); Social Security card or application; employment authorization document (EAD); proof of arrival date

name: USCRI Preferred Communities Program — Intensive Case Management for Vulnerable Refugees
organization: U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants (USCRI)
description: The USCRI Preferred Communities Program, funded by the Office of Refugee Resettlement (ORR), provides intensive, individualized case management to the most vulnerable refugees resettled in the United States. Operating at 19 sites in 14 states, the program serves refugees who face significant barriers to self-sufficiency, including those with serious medical conditions, disabilities, single parents with young children, elderly refugees, and survivors of torture or trauma. Case managers work one-on-one with participants for up to one year from arrival, coordinating access to medical care, mental health services, housing assistance, public benefits enrollment, English language classes, employment readiness, and community integration. The program is specifically designed for refugees whose complex needs require more support than standard resettlement programs provide.
eligibility: Refugees identified as highly vulnerable during resettlement, including individuals with serious medical conditions, physical or mental disabilities, single-parent families, elderly refugees, survivors of torture or trauma, and large families; must be within one year of arrival in the US; referrals typically come through resettlement agencies
amount: No direct cash grants to individuals; program provides intensive case management, service coordination, and referrals to benefits and resources at no cost
applicationProcess: Referrals are typically made through USCRI resettlement offices and partner agencies during the initial resettlement process. Refugees identified as having complex needs or heightened vulnerability are enrolled in the Preferred Communities program for intensive case management. Contact your local USCRI office or resettlement agency to inquire about eligibility and enrollment.
geographicScope: United States — 19 sites in 14 states through USCRI field offices (including Albany NY, Cleveland OH, Des Moines IA, Erie PA, Raleigh NC, and others)
documentsRequired: Refugee admission documentation (I-94, refugee travel document); medical records if applicable; resettlement agency referral; specific documentation varies by site

name: Canada Settlement Program — Language, Employment & Community Integration for Newcomers
description: The Canada Settlement Program, administered by Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), provides a comprehensive range of free services to help newcomers integrate into Canadian society. The program funds service provider organizations across Canada (outside Quebec, which operates its own program) to deliver language training (LINC — Language Instruction for Newcomers to Canada), employment-related services, community connections, and information and orientation about life in Canada. Newcomers can access needs assessments, referrals to community resources, language classes at multiple proficiency levels, job search workshops, credential recognition guidance, mentorship programs, and support connecting with established community members. Services are available in person and online. The program is distinct from the Resettlement Assistance Program (RAP), which covers only the first few weeks; the Settlement Program supports newcomers throughout their longer-term integration process.
eligibility: Permanent residents of Canada; protected persons (convention refugees and persons in need of protection); individuals approved for permanent residence but who have not yet received their permanent resident status; temporary residents with a work or study permit who are transitioning to permanent residence are also eligible for some services
amount: No direct cash grants to individuals; all settlement services are provided free of charge through IRCC-funded organizations
applicationProcess: Contact any IRCC-funded settlement service provider in your area. You can find local services through the IRCC website or by calling 1-888-242-2100. Start with a needs assessment to identify which services will help you most. No appointment is needed for most information sessions. Language classes (LINC) require a language assessment through a designated centre. All services are free for eligible newcomers.
geographicScope: Canada — nationwide excluding Quebec (which operates its own provincial integration program); services available in all provinces and territories through a network of funded service providers
documentsRequired: Proof of immigration status (permanent resident card, confirmation of permanent residence, protected person status document, or valid work/study permit); proof of identity; no income verification required — services are universally free for eligible newcomers

name: UK Asylum Support (Section 95) — Housing & Subsistence for Asylum Seekers
description: UK Asylum Support under Section 95 of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 provides housing and financial subsistence to asylum seekers in the United Kingdom who would otherwise be destitute. The Home Office provides dispersal accommodation — fully furnished housing in various locations across the UK — along with a weekly cash allowance for food, clothing, and other essential living costs. As of 2025, the weekly allowance is approximately £49.18 per person. Accommodation is provided on a no-choice basis, meaning recipients cannot choose their location, and is intended to be temporary until the asylum claim is decided. Asylum seekers who are pregnant or have children under 3 may receive additional support. The program also includes Section 98 (emergency/initial accommodation) for those who need immediate housing while their Section 95 application is processed, and Section 4 support for failed asylum seekers who face genuine obstacles to leaving the UK.
eligibility: Asylum seekers in the United Kingdom who have an active asylum claim and are destitute or at risk of becoming destitute (having less than £5 available and no adequate accommodation); failed asylum seekers may qualify for Section 4 support if they face barriers to departure
amount: Weekly allowance of approximately £49.18 per person for food, clothing, and essentials; fully furnished accommodation provided at no cost; additional maternity payment of £300 available
applicationProcess: Apply for asylum support by completing form ASF1 (available on gov.uk) and submitting it by post or through your legal representative. You must first register your asylum claim with the Home Office. If you need immediate emergency accommodation, request Section 98 support. The Home Office will assess whether you are destitute. If approved, you will be assigned dispersal accommodation and begin receiving the weekly allowance. Processing typically takes several weeks; emergency support can begin immediately.
geographicScope: United Kingdom — dispersal accommodation available across England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland; locations are assigned by the Home Office
documentsRequired: Completed ASF1 application form; proof of asylum claim (Application Registration Card); evidence of destitution (bank statements showing less than £5 available); proof of identity; any evidence of special needs (medical conditions, pregnancy, children)
